strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: obtaining uncertainty estimates from pretrained contrastive VLMs without retraining their encoders. Applying last-layer Laplace approximations to both modalities provides a coherent approach.
The evaluation spans five zero-shot classification datasets, multiple active-learning domains, and CLIP and SigLIP models, with additional CLIP-Huge results in the appendix.
There are useful empirical calibration improvements for CLIP. For example, BayesVLM reduces EuroSAT NLPD from 2.16 to 1.90 and CIFAR-100 ECE from 6.31% to 2.69%, while largely preserving accuracy.

Applying the cosine-similarity approximation to PCME++ improves its reported NLPD and ECE across all five datasets. The targeted-selection baselines also help distinguish some benefits of targeting from uncertainty-based acquisition.
weaknesses: The central cosine-similarity derivation contains invalid equalities. Equation (56) replaces the expectation of a ratio with a ratio of expectations, although the numerator and norms are dependent; Equation (62) similarly replaces random denominators with their expectations. Consequently, Equations (12) and (65) are heuristic variance approximations, not exact identities. The paper needs explicit approximation assumptions and quantitative error analysis. The limited 500-sample experiment with shifted means does not establish reliability across realistic covariance and uncertainty regimes.

The Bayesian formulation has unresolved technical problems. The marginal-likelihood objective in Equations (27)–(28) omits the prior density at the expansion point and uses determinants rather than log-determinants. As written, it cannot justify the claimed evidence-based prior tuning. Furthermore, the dense embedding covariances in Equations (9)–(10) become diagonal in Section 3.3 without evaluating the information discarded. These issues undermine the claimed principled uncertainty propagation.

The calibration comparisons provide weaker support than the claims suggest. Against temperature-scaled CLIP, gains are mixed: BayesVLM has worse NLPD on CIFAR-100 and DTD and worse ECE on Flowers-102. SigLIP improvements are generally small, with ECE worsening on two datasets. Temperature scaling catastrophically degrades SigLIP on several datasets, which requires investigation before treating it as a convincing baseline. PCME++ also uses a different backbone and training data, confounding attribution of the large performance gap.

The active-learning evaluation does not convincingly isolate the proposed uncertainty model. Targeted entropy is competitive with, and sometimes better than, BALD or EPIG in the displayed curves. There are no comparisons with stronger diversity-based or VLM-specific acquisition methods, and repeated-run uncertainty is not clearly reported for the proposed methods. Domain-specific labeled validation sets are used for checkpoint and EPIG hyperparameter selection, but their sizes and contribution to the labeling budget are unspecified.

Several inconsistencies obstruct reproduction: Hessian estimation uses 30,000 pairs in Section 4 versus 327,680 in Appendix D.1; pseudo-count search ranges differ; Section 4.1 selects the highest NLPD whereas Appendix D.2 minimizes it; the main-text and appendix online updates use different normalization factors; and Equation (72) reverses the BALD entropy difference relative to Equation (14). These discrepancies need resolution to establish which algorithm produced the results.

The contribution primarily combines established last-layer Laplace, Kronecker curvature, probit prediction, and Bayesian acquisition methods. Stronger ablations against simpler covariance or uncertainty approximations are needed to establish the value of the specific combination. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent despite efficiency claims, and broad reliability claims rest partly on a single qualitative corruption example.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: adding uncertainty estimates to pretrained contrastive VLMs without retraining their encoders. Combining last-layer Laplace inference with analytic uncertainty propagation provides a potentially useful approach.

The experiments demonstrate meaningful calibration improvements over vanilla CLIP on five datasets. For example, Food-101 ECE decreases from 3.91% to 0.79%, while predictive accuracy is largely preserved.

The active-learning evaluation covers multiple domains and includes additional CLIP-Huge and SigLIP results. Targeted random and entropy baselines help distinguish the benefits of targeting from those of uncertainty-based acquisition.
weaknesses: The central cosine-similarity derivation is mathematically unjustified as written. Equations (56) and (62) replace expectations of ratios with ratios of expectations, although the numerator and denominator are dependent. Consequently, the variance in Equations (12)/(65) is an approximation, not the stated equality. No error analysis or sufficient conditions justify neglecting denominator fluctuations. The qualitative comparison using 500 samples from one input with shifted means is insufficient to establish reliability across the claimed settings.

The uncertainty propagation introduces additional unvalidated assumptions. Equations (9)–(10) generally produce dense embedding covariances, whereas Section 3.3 assumes diagonal covariance without explaining or evaluating this transition. Independence between the image and text projection parameters is also imposed despite their joint contrastive training. Ablations against posterior Monte Carlo prediction and alternative covariance approximations are needed to establish whether the reported uncertainties faithfully represent the proposed posterior.

Several equations essential to implementation are incorrect or inconsistent. The marginal-likelihood objective in Equations (27)–(28) omits the log-prior term and uses a determinant product rather than its logarithm. Equation (72) reverses the BALD entropy difference relative to Equation (14). The online factor updates use different normalizations in the main text and appendix. These could include transcription errors, but without clarification they undermine confidence in the implemented inference and acquisition procedures.

The zero-shot comparisons provide weaker evidence than the claims suggest. Against temperature-scaled CLIP, gains are mixed: BayesVLM has worse Flowers-102 ECE and worse CIFAR-100 and DTD NLPD. SigLIP improvements are small, and ECE worsens on two datasets. The extreme deterioration of temperature-scaled SigLIP, such as Food-101 ECE increasing from 1.66% to 65.83%, requires investigation. PCME++ uses a different backbone and training history, so its substantially lower accuracy does not isolate uncertainty-estimation quality.

The active-learning evidence does not adequately establish the incremental contribution of Bayesian uncertainty. Targeted entropy is competitive in several plots, stronger diversity-based and VLM-specific acquisition baselines are absent, and the number of repeated runs and uncertainty across runs are unclear. Domain-specific labeled validation sets are used for checkpoint selection and EPIG hyperparameter tuning, but their sizes and annotation costs are not reported. This limits interpretation of the claimed sample efficiency.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are incomplete. Section 4 reports 30k image-text pairs for Hessian estimation, whereas Appendix D.1 reports 327,680. Hyperparameter search ranges and whether NLPD is minimized or maximized also differ between sections. The code-availability statement contains no link. Runtime, memory, Hessian-estimation cost, and acquisition overhead are not quantified despite efficiency being a central motivation.

The contribution mainly combines established Laplace, Kronecker-factorization, probit, BALD/EPIG, and nearest-neighbor components; its strongest methodological distinction therefore depends on validating the cosine approximation. Broader claims concerning interpretable uncertainty, distribution shift, and safety-critical utility are supported primarily by one corrupted example rather than systematic uncertainty or selective-prediction benchmarks. Overall, the promising empirical results do not overcome the unresolved technical and evaluation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: adding uncertainty estimates to pretrained contrastive VLMs without retraining their encoders. Restricting the Laplace approximation to projection layers makes the approach potentially useful.

The CLIP results provide positive evidence for calibration improvements. For example, BayesVLM reduces EuroSAT NLPD from 2.16 to 1.90 and Food-101 ECE from 3.91% to 0.79%, while largely preserving classification accuracy.

The evaluation includes multiple classification datasets, cross-domain active learning, and supplementary experiments with CLIP-Huge and SigLIP. Including targeted random and targeted entropy baselines helps assess the contribution beyond nearest-neighbor targeting.
Applying the cosine-similarity approximation to PCME++ also improves its reported calibration, suggesting that this component could have utility beyond the proposed posterior approximation.
weaknesses: The central cosine-distribution derivation contains unjustified equalities. Equation (56) replaces the expectation of a ratio with a ratio of expectations, despite dependence between the numerator and norms; Equation (62) similarly replaces random squared norms by their expectations. Consequently, Equations (12) and (65) are approximations, not exact variances. The paper needs explicit assumptions and broader quantitative error analysis, particularly because the diagonal-covariance assumption also discards correlations present in Equations (9)–(10). A single KDE comparison with shifted means is insufficient to establish reliability.

The marginal-likelihood objective used to learn prior precision is incorrect as written in Equations (27)–(28): it omits the log prior at the MAP estimate and subtracts a product of determinants rather than the corresponding log-determinant terms. These omissions materially affect optimization of the prior precision. Clarifying whether this is only a presentation error or also affects implementation is necessary to assess the posterior estimates.

The calibration comparisons do not convincingly establish a substantial advantage over strong matched baselines. Improvements over temperature-scaled CLIP are modest and mixed; SigLIP gains are small, with worse ECE on Flowers-102 and Food-101. Temperature scaling catastrophically degrades SigLIP on several datasets, warranting investigation of the calibration protocol. PCME++ uses a different backbone and training setup, so its much lower accuracy confounds conclusions about uncertainty quality.

The active-learning evaluation needs stronger controls and clearer accounting. It uses unlabeled test inputs for selection and labeled domain-specific validation sets for checkpoint and EPIG hyperparameter selection, but does not specify validation sizes or account for this supervision in the label budget. Comparisons with diversity-based or contemporary VLM active-learning methods are missing, and the number of repeated runs and uncertainty for the proposed methods are unclear. Ablations should separate acquisition, posterior prediction, and online updating.

Several inconsistencies prevent confident reproduction: Hessian estimation uses 30k pairs in the main text versus 327,680 in Appendix D.1; posterior-factor updates use different normalizations in Equations (17)–(18) and (84)–(85); and Equation (72) reverses the sign of BALD relative to Equation (14). Hyperparameter selection descriptions also disagree. The reproducibility statement ends without an actual code link.

Claims of efficiency, broad applicability, and reliable uncertainty under distribution shift exceed the evidence. No runtime or memory measurements substantiate efficiency; access to representative pretraining data remains a substantial requirement; and corruption robustness is illustrated using only one example. The contribution primarily combines established Laplace, Kronecker-factorization, and Bayesian acquisition techniques, making rigorous validation of the new approximation especially important.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical problem: adding uncertainty estimates to pretrained contrastive vision-language models without retraining their encoders. Combining projection-layer Laplace approximations with analytic prediction is computationally attractive.
CLIP-base calibration results are promising: BayesVLM achieves lower ECE than all reported baselines on all seven datasets in Table 2, generally preserving classification accuracy.

Experiments cover several model sizes, SigLIP, probabilistic embedding models, and cross-domain active learning. PCME++ results show consistent NLPD and ECE improvements, and the active-learning curves demonstrate useful gains over several random and entropy baselines.
Reported inference overhead is small: approximately 4.7% for CLIP-base and 0.35% for CLIP-huge. Algorithms and extensive appendices provide useful methodological detail.
weaknesses: The central ProbCosine derivation contains invalid equalities. Equation (52) replaces an expectation of a ratio with a ratio of expectations, despite dependence between the numerator and norms; Equation (58) similarly replaces random denominators by their expectations. Consequently, Equations (8) and (61) are approximations, not exact variances. No error bounds or clear concentration conditions justify these substitutions. Figure 9 provides only a limited qualitative comparison using 500 samples, without systematic tests across covariance scales and anisotropy.

The stated marginal-likelihood objective in Equation (24) is incorrect: it omits the prior density at the fitted parameters and uses a product of determinants instead of the corresponding log-determinant contribution. These are consequential omissions because this objective determines the prior precision. Moreover, Equation (6) produces generally dense embedding covariances, whereas ProbCosine assumes diagonal covariances, without adequately explaining or evaluating this additional approximation.

Active-learning comparisons do not isolate the benefit of the uncertainty estimator. EPIG uses sequential model and curvature updates, whereas the entropy and BALD descriptions select top-scoring batches without equivalent updates. EPIG additionally tunes two parameters using domain-specific labeled validation data, whose size and contribution to the annotation budget are unspecified. Stronger diversity-based baselines, matched update protocols, and repeated-run uncertainty estimates are needed.

Claims of consistent improvement overstate the results. Table 2 shows accuracy decreases on four datasets and mixed NLPD comparisons against temperature scaling. For SigLIP, ECE worsens relative to the original model on four of seven datasets, including FOOD-101 from 1.66 to 4.87. ProLIP calibration also worsens on three datasets. These results materially limit the claimed generality, especially when the original pretraining distribution is unavailable.

The evidence does not sufficiently distinguish useful epistemic uncertainty from input-dependent confidence rescaling. Missing ablations include mean correction versus variance correction, image-only versus text-only uncertainty, and analytic prediction versus posterior sampling. Aggregate calibration and one corruption example provide limited support for broader domain-shift and safety-critical claims.

The contribution largely combines established last-layer Laplace, KFAC, probit prediction, BALD, and EPIG techniques. The VLM application is useful, but the distinctive cosine approximation and its empirical advantage need stronger validation to establish a contribution competitive with the acceptance threshold.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the code-availability statement contains no URL; acquisition Monte Carlo sample counts, active-learning repetition counts, and precise data splits are not adequately specified. Equation (68) reverses the BALD entropy difference relative to Equation (10). The cost of estimating curvature from 327,680 image-text pairs and of active acquisition is also unreported, despite the emphasis on efficiency.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: adding uncertainty estimates to pretrained vision-language models without retraining their encoders. Combining last-layer Laplace approximation with analytic uncertainty propagation is practically appealing, and the reported inference overhead is small.
The CLIP-Base calibration results are encouraging. In Table 2, BayesVLM improves ECE over all listed baselines on all seven datasets and reduces NLPD relative to vanilla CLIP across the benchmarks.

The evaluation covers multiple model architectures, classification datasets, and active-learning settings. Applying ProbCosine to existing probabilistic models, particularly PCME++, provides additional evidence of practical utility.
weaknesses: The central ProbCosine derivation contains unjustified equalities. Equation (52) replaces the expectation of a ratio with a ratio of expectations, although the numerator and random norms are dependent. Equations (58) and (61) similarly treat random denominators as fixed without accounting for their contribution to variance. These may serve as heuristics under norm concentration, but the paper provides neither conditions nor error analysis. Moreover, Equation (6) generally produces dense embedding covariances, whereas ProbCosine assumes diagonal covariances without clearly specifying or evaluating this additional approximation. Figure 9 offers only a narrow qualitative check.

The posterior-fitting objective is incorrect as written. Equation (24) omits the parameter log-prior and subtracts a product of determinants rather than the corresponding log-determinant contribution. The omitted prior terms depend on the precision being optimized, so this directly affects the claimed marginal-likelihood optimization. The pretrained parameters also need not remain a posterior mode after changing the prior or substituting a proxy dataset. The manuscript needs to establish which objective was implemented and justify the resulting posterior approximation.

Several performance claims overstate the evidence. Table 2 does not show consistent accuracy improvements: BayesVLM is below vanilla CLIP on four of seven datasets, and temperature scaling achieves lower NLPD on three. In Table 9, BayesVLM worsens SigLIP ECE on four of seven datasets, including Food-101 from 1.66 to 4.87 and ImageNet-R from 1.36 to 3.96. These results support useful CLIP calibration gains, but not the broad claims of consistent improvements across architectures and metrics.

The active-learning experiments do not convincingly isolate the contribution of Bayesian uncertainty. Targeted entropy is often competitive with BALD and EPIG in Figure 3, while EPIG additionally receives online posterior updates and validation-based hyperparameter tuning. Stronger acquisition baselines, such as diversity or core-set selection, are absent. Repeated-run uncertainty is not established for the Bayesian acquisition curves. Controlled comparisons using matched targeting, update procedures, and tuning budgets are needed.

The contribution beyond established last-layer Laplace, KFAC, probit prediction, BALD, and EPIG is insufficiently validated. In particular, there are no decisive ablations separating the effects of the probabilistic cosine mean, variance correction, and posterior covariance structure from simpler confidence rescaling. Stabilization of the Hessian trace does not establish that its inverse, or the resulting predictive uncertainties, is accurately estimated. The single-example corruption illustration also provides limited support for broad distribution-shift and safety-critical claims.

Reproducibility is weakened by consequential inconsistencies. The code-availability statement ends without a link; Equation (68) reverses the BALD sign relative to Equation (10); and Section 4.2 says the selected pseudo-data count maximizes NLPD, whereas Appendix E.2 says it minimizes NLPD. The number of acquisition Monte Carlo samples and repeated active-learning runs is not clearly specified. These ambiguities make it difficult to determine whether the mathematical problems are presentation errors or affect the reported implementation.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: adding uncertainty estimates to pretrained vision-language models without retraining their encoders. Combining projection-layer Laplace approximations with analytical prediction is practically appealing.
CLIP-Base calibration results are strong: Table 2 reports lower ECE than all listed baselines on all seven datasets, while largely preserving classification accuracy.

The evaluation covers multiple model sizes, CLIP and SigLIP, seven classification benchmarks, and several active learning tasks. Applying ProbCosine to ProLIP and PCME++ provides additional evidence of its usefulness.
Reported inference overhead is modest—approximately 4.7% for CLIP-Base and 0.35% for CLIP-Huge—and the active learning results show promising gains over random and entropy-based selection.
weaknesses: The central ProbCosine derivation contains unjustified equalities. Equations (52) and (58) replace expectations of ratios with ratios of expectations, although the numerator and random norms are dependent. Equation (8) consequently gives an approximate variance, not the stated exact variance. Such approximations may work under norm concentration, but the paper provides neither conditions nor quantitative error analysis. Figure 9 offers only a limited qualitative comparison and labels values outside [-1,1] as cosine similarities without explaining the scaling.

The posterior construction has unresolved technical inconsistencies. Equation (24), used to optimize prior precision, omits the log prior at the expansion point and uses a product of determinants rather than its logarithm; as written, it is not the Laplace log marginal likelihood. Moreover, Equation (6) generally produces full embedding covariances, whereas ProbCosine assumes diagonal covariances, without clearly specifying or validating this additional approximation. These issues affect the reproducibility and interpretation of the uncertainty estimates.

Claims of consistent improvement overstate the evidence. In Table 2, BayesVLM reduces accuracy relative to vanilla CLIP on four of seven datasets, and temperature scaling obtains better NLPD on several datasets. For SigLIP, Table 9 shows worse ECE than the unmodified model on four of seven datasets, including FOOD-101 increasing from 1.66 to 4.87. The strongest supported conclusion is improved CLIP calibration, rather than broadly improved accuracy and calibration across VLMs.

The comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution beyond established last-layer Laplace inference and confidence rescaling. Missing ablations include image-only versus text-only uncertainty, simpler covariance structures, and Monte Carlo prediction from the same posterior. Comparisons with relevant probabilistic adapters and stronger VLM calibration methods would better establish the significance of the proposed combination.

The active learning evidence needs stronger controls. EPIG receives online parameter and Hessian updates, but equivalent updates for the competing acquisition strategies are not established. Selection uses the unlabeled evaluation inputs, making this a transductive setting whose conclusions should be scoped accordingly. The paper also does not clearly report repeated-run variability for the proposed acquisition methods or compare against strong diversity-based acquisition baselines. Equation (68) reverses the BALD sign relative to Equation (10), leaving an implementation-critical ambiguity.

Important reproducibility and efficiency details remain incomplete. The code-availability statement ends without a link; Monte Carlo sample counts, active learning repetitions, and precise data splits are insufficiently specified. Section 4.2 selects the highest NLPD while Appendix E.2 specifies the minimum. Inference timing excludes the setup cost of processing approximately 327,000 image-text pairs and tuning hyperparameters on labeled ImageNet data. These limitations, together with the mathematical issues, prevent the otherwise promising empirical results from meeting the acceptance threshold.
